text: A psalm. Sing to the LORD a new song, for he has done wonders; his right hand and his holy arm have won him victory.
The LORD has made his salvation known; he has revealed his righteousness before the eyes of the nations.
He has remembered his mercy and his faithfulness to the house of Israel; all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.
Shout to the LORD, all the earth; break forth, sing for joy, and make music.
Make music to the LORD with the lyre, with the lyre and the sound of song.

versions.text: Make music to the LORD with the harp, with the harp and the sound of song.
versions.explanation: The kinnor is a stringed lyre; 'lyre' is more precise, and it also avoids the slightly flat repetition of 'harp' in English while preserving the Hebrew's deliberate repetition.

text: With trumpets and the sound of the ram's horn, shout before the King, the LORD.
Let the sea roar, and everything in it, the world and all who live in it.
Let the rivers clap their hands, let the mountains sing together for joy—

versions.text: Let the rivers clap their hands, let the mountains sing together for joy
versions.explanation: The verse runs on into verse 9 with no punctuation at all. Adding a dash (or comma) at the end signals the continuation for oral reading.

text: before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness and the peoples with equity.

versions.text: before the LORD, for he is coming to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness and the peoples with fairness.
versions.explanation: 'Equity' better renders מֵישָׁרִים (uprightness/straightness in judgment) than the weaker 'fairness'; 'he comes' is tighter for oral reading and matches the perfect-as-prophetic sense.
